info.description:
The JSON API a browser and an automation client both drive (JD-016).

Every endpoint lives under /api. Authenticate either with the session
cookie POST /api/auth/login sets, or with a bearer token created by
`jaildeck token add <name>`. The Authorization header takes precedence
over the cookie, and a bad token returns 401 rather than falling back to
one, so a token client fails cleanly even while a session is active.

Swagger 2.0 cannot describe a cookie as a security scheme, so only the
bearer token appears below. The cookie works on every endpoint the token
does.

The version here is the API's and is bumped with the changelog at
release time; it is not read from the binary.
info.title: Jail Deck API

get.description:
Redirects to /api/jails, so a client that guessed the base path lands on
something rather than a 404. It is behind authentication like everything
else here, so an unauthenticated caller gets 401 instead of the redirect.

What Jail Deck did: timestamp, operation, target, the command it ran, exit
code and whether it timed out (JD-011). Filters combine, and all of them
are applied to the whole file rather than to the page.

The log lives in /var/log and is rotated by newsyslog, so after a rotation
this sees only the current file. History appears to truncate with nothing
in the response to say so: that is the accepted cost of treating a log as
a log.

400.description: A filter that cannot be parsed

post.description:
Sets an HttpOnly, Secure, SameSite=Strict session cookie. Secure means a
browser discards it over plain HTTP on a non-loopback origin, so reach a
remote host through an SSH forward rather than binding it to 0.0.0.0 (JD-002).

Clears the cookie and forgets the session server-side. Harmless without
one, so a client that has already lost its cookie can still call it.

get.description:
Says whether this request arrived as a session or a token, and when a
session expires. Sessions live in memory, so restarting the service signs
every browser out; tokens are stored and survive.

401.description: Neither a session nor a token

get.description:
Whether <pool>/jails and its media, templates and containers children
exist and where they are mounted (JD-006, JD-021). Read-only.

put.description:
Idempotent: creates only what is absent and reports what it made. It
refuses when a dataset on another pool is already mounted where a missing
one would go, because creating it would mount over that pool and over any
jails inside it (JD-021).

get.description:
Every check this host must pass before it can run jails, each pass, fail
or unknown with what was observed and the remedy. Nothing here writes: a
check that cannot observe reports unknown rather than failing the request.

Running jails from jls merged with configured ones from jail.conf and
jail.conf.d, so a stopped jail is listed too — seeing it is how you start
it (JD-004).

Each jail carries its ZFS storage: datasets mounted at its path or under
it, and the user properties of its own dataset. Sizes are bytes, not the
1.41G zfs prints, so they can be compared and totalled.

Both keys are absent for a jail with no dataset — and also when the pool
could not be read, which is logged at WARN rather than failing the
request, so an unreadable pool never costs you the list (JD-022).

The same shape as an element of the listing, storage included. It reads
that same merged listing rather than asking for a single jail, because a
jail present only in jls or only in configuration must still be found.

put.description:
201 when it was created, 200 when it was already there, 409 when it
exists at a different mountpoint. Idempotent, so a client that timed out
repeats the call and the answer says where it stands (JD-016).

Five native properties may be set — mountpoint, refquota, recordsize,
compression, atime — out of the sixty-odd ZFS calls editable. Anything
else is 400 naming the list: sharenfs would export the jail's data and
canmount would stop it mounting. quota is deliberately absent, because
JD-007 puts the limit on refquota.

mountpoint may be set only at creation; asking for one an existing dataset
does not have is a 409 with both values rather than a move (JD-023).

Values are not validated here. zfs answers recordsize=7K with "must be
power of 2 from 512B to 16M", and that sentence comes back — as a 400, so
a client does not retry a value that can never work.
put.summary: Create or update a child dataset

400.description: A property outside the allowlist, or a value zfs refused

404.description: No such jail, or it is not on ZFS

409.description: It exists at a different mountpoint

patch.description:
The same as tagging the jail, on a dataset beneath its own.

Worth keeping separate: a jail's listing reports its own dataset's
properties, never a child's. Tag a child with otter:instance and it will
not appear on the jail — by design, or one jail with three children would
look like four instances to a client searching by tag (JD-022).

parameters.description: Property names to values; null removes
parameters.name: properties

post.description:
The same three commands in the other direction.

It need not be the jail it left, and it need not keep the name it left
with: a dataset retained from ottermq can come back as ottermq-2's data,
which is the point of keeping it. Its properties and snapshots travel with
it, because they belong to the dataset and not to where it sits.

from is the short name from GET /retained, not the full dataset path.

parameters.description: The name it will have in this jail
parameters.name: child

parameters.description: Which retained dataset to bring back
parameters.name: source

409.description: The jail already has a child of that name

post.description:
Moves it to <pool>/jails/retained/<name>. zfs destroy -r on a jail takes
its children and their snapshots with it (JD-007), so a dataset worth
keeping has to stop being a child first.

Three audited commands: zfs rename -u, zfs unmount, zfs mount. The -u is
not optional — a plain zfs rename unmounts and remounts inside the same
command, which on a running jail is the filesystem vanishing from under a
live process (JD-025).

It still unmounts: remounted=true means the filesystem moved and a running
jail just lost that path, so stop it first. Leaving the move half done is
worse — a dataset still mounted inside a jail makes the jail undestroyable.

The retained parent is created on demand and is deliberately not part of
the layout readiness check (JD-021).
post.summary: Retain a dataset past its jail

parameters.description: The name it will have under retained
parameters.name: target

put.description:
No -r, no children. Use it when the thing worth snapshotting is the data
and not the userland: a jail's root is a clone of a template and can be
made again, which is the premise of JD-007.

delete.description:
As above, on one dataset only. Same clone and hold refusals, same
full-name confirm.

post.description:
The route that matters for a jail whose state lives in a child: rolling
the data back without touching the userland.

parameters.description: Accept losing the snapshots taken after it
parameters.name: destroy_newer

patch.description:
Sets ZFS user properties on the jail's own dataset — the tags the listing
reads back (JD-004). Returns what the dataset carries afterwards, read
from ZFS rather than assumed.

PATCH, not PUT: these merge. A replacing write would strip a tag another
tool had set, and zrepl:placeholder and com.sun:auto-snapshot both live in
this namespace on real hosts.

A null value removes the property via zfs inherit, which is not the same
as setting it empty. Only user properties — the name must contain a colon
— and the value is passed through untouched (JD-011).

parameters.description: Property names to values; null removes
parameters.name: properties

400.description: A name that is not a user property

404.description: No such jail, or it is not on ZFS

post.description:
Runs service jail restart.
A client disconnecting does not abort the operation: the command is
detached from request cancellation and still bounded by its own timeout
(JD-014). Audited either way.

504.description: Timed out and may still be running

get.description:
The jail's own dataset and its children's, oldest first.

Ordered by create_txg, ZFS's transaction group, not by created. A
timestamp has second granularity and two snapshots taken in the same
second tie on it — and "which is newer" is exactly what decides what a
rollback destroys. The transaction group never ties.

name is the full dataset@snapshot, which is what confirm must equal
elsewhere; short is the part after the @, which goes in a URL.

Unfiltered. On a host running zrepl this is long — one jail on the
deployment target has 39 snapshots, 35 of them hourly.

404.description: No such jail, or it is not on ZFS

put.description:
201 when taken, 200 with existed=true when it was already there, so the
retry after a timeout does not raise zfs's "dataset already exists".

The jail route is recursive: zfs snapshot -r takes the jail's dataset
and every child at ONE point in time, which is what lets a root be
re-cloned while its data stays consistent with it (JD-007, JD-024).

parameters.description: Snapshot name, the part after the @
parameters.name: snapshot

404.description: No such jail, or it is not on ZFS

delete.description:
Recursive, matching what the recursive create made.

409 with a dependent clone or a hold, naming them. Both are checked by
asking ZFS first — zfs get clones and zfs holds — rather than by running
the destroy and reading its complaint, so the refusal happens before
anything destructive does. Neither can be overridden here: getting past a
clone needs zfs destroy -R, which takes the clone with it (JD-024).

confirm must be the snapshot's FULL dataset@snapshot, not the word in the
path, so a script looping over jails with one snapshot name in a variable
cannot confirm every one of them by accident (JD-016).

409.description: A clone or a hold is in the way

post.description:
NEVER recursive. zfs rollback has no way to descend into children, and its
own -r means something else entirely — "destroy the snapshots newer than
this one". So this rolls back the jail's own dataset and leaves its
children where they are; a child is rolled back through its own route, as
a separate decision (JD-024).

409 when newer snapshots exist, naming every one it would destroy. Pass
destroy_newer=true to accept losing exactly those — the refusal comes
first so the second call is informed rather than a retry with more force.

Still 409, even with destroy_newer=true, when one of those newer snapshots
is held or has a clone.

parameters.description: Accept losing the snapshots taken after it
parameters.name: destroy_newer

409.description: Newer snapshots, a clone or a hold

post.description:
Runs service jail start.
A client disconnecting does not abort the operation: the command is
detached from request cancellation and still bounded by its own timeout
(JD-014). Audited either way.

504.description: Timed out and may still be running

post.description:
Runs service jail stop. Anything running inside is interrupted.
A client disconnecting does not abort the operation: the command is
detached from request cancellation and still bounded by its own timeout
(JD-014). Audited either way.

504.description: Timed out and may still be running

get.description:
Everything under <pool>/jails/retained, with the short name a restore
asks for. Without this a client that retained something has no way to find
it again, and the whole point of retaining is that the jail it belonged to
is gone (JD-025).

Empty on a host that has never retained anything, rather than an error:
the retained dataset is created on demand.

request_id.description:
RequestID is the caller's X-Request-Id, omitted when it sent none
(JD-011: nothing is stored that the request did not supply).

observed.description:
Observed is what the host actually said, empty when nothing could be
observed.

remedy.description:
Remedy is set on every failed check and only there: a command for a
root shell where one exists, otherwise the file or setting to change.

mountpoint_taken_by.description:
MountpointTakenBy is set on a missing dataset when another dataset, on
any pool, already has its expected mountpoint. Ensure refuses then.

used.description:
Bytes, not the "1.41G" zfs list prints by default, so a client can
compare and total them.

conflict.description:
Conflict is set when the dataset exists somewhere other than where the
request said. Mountpoint is settable only at creation (JD-023), so this
is not a change the API will make -- and reporting both values says more
than refusing would.

remounted.description:
Remounted says whether the filesystem was actually carried to the new
mountpoint. False when the dataset was not mounted to begin with --
which is not a failure, just nothing to carry.

datasets.description:
Datasets and Properties are filled by the listing and by GET
/api/jails/{name}, and left out everywhere else. omitempty rather than an
empty collection on purpose: a start or restart response reports what the
operation knew, and claiming "datasets: []" there would say the jail has
none when the truth is that nothing looked.

create_txg.description:
CreateTXG is ZFS's transaction group: the only exact ordering. Two
snapshots taken in the same second share a Created, so a client deciding
which is newer has to compare this instead.

name.description:
Name is "dataset@snapshot" as zfs prints it, and is what confirm= must
equal on a destroy or a rollback (JD-024).

short.description: Short is the part after the @, which is what the URL carries.

BearerAuth.description: Type "Bearer " followed by a token from `jaildeck token add`.
BearerAuth.name: Authorization
